items.text: Procrastination means choosing short-term comfort. Autistic inertia is when the distress of being stuck is worse than doing the thing — and you still can't move.
items.rationale: Sharpest compression of the briefing's core insight. The contrast between the two definitions does the emotional work — self-blame dissolves when the mechanism is named this precisely. Scroll-stopper.

items.text: Autistic inertia isn't avoidance. It's a nervous-system state where intention and action become decoupled. You know exactly what you need to do. Your body just won't.
items.rationale: Different entry point into the same angle — leads with the body/intention split rather than the procrastination contrast. Works for people who've never heard 'inertia' used this way, and doesn't overlap structurally with post 1.

items.text: 'Just rest' isn't the whole answer for autistic burnout. Rest lowers the load. But the nervous system also needs sensory pleasure, special-interest time — small doses of actually feeling alive.
items.rationale: Validates a lived frustration without dismissing rest as useless. The phrase 'actually feeling alive' is resonant and specific. Speaks to people who've been resting for months and still feel hollow — a very common and rarely named experience.

items.text: AuDHD burnout recovery is its own puzzle: enough novelty for the ADHD brain, enough predictability for the autistic one. They don't always agree on what that looks like.
items.rationale: Lands the AuDHD-specific tension in one sentence. Practical because it implies active calibration is required — not just rest — without being prescriptive. Short enough to be quotable.

items.text: Being AuDHD isn't two diagnoses stacked. It's a specific internal conflict: the ADHD brain wants novelty and chaos; the autistic nervous system desperately needs predictability. Nobody wins cleanly.
items.rationale: 'Nobody wins cleanly' is dry community-native humor, not a brand voice. The semicolon structure mirrors the tension being described. Shareable because it's precise enough to feel true rather than generic.

items.text: AuDHD, explained: two neurotypes, one nervous system, negotiating constantly. The ADHD side wants to flip the table. The autistic side already mapped where everything goes.
items.rationale: Wry and absurdist — a different flavor from post 5. The image of 'already mapped where everything goes' is concrete and funny in a way that lands as recognition, not mockery. Strong alternate or companion post.

items.text: 70% of neurodivergent employees are afraid to disclose at work — up from 60% last year. 79% report stigma when requesting accommodations. The fear isn't irrational. The data agrees.
items.rationale: The closing sentence does the emotional lift without editorializing excessively. Data is sourced directly from Forbes June 2026 survey — defensible as stated. Validates a fear people are frequently told to push past.

items.text: Under the ADA, you describe your functional needs when requesting workplace accommodations — not necessarily your diagnosis. HR gets what it needs to act. Your medical history stays yours.
items.rationale: Immediately actionable, information most workers genuinely don't have. Framed as information rather than legal advice. 'Stays yours' is the reassuring payoff that makes people want to share it.
items.sensitivity_flag: Describes ADA rights in simplified plain language — stops short of legal advice, but 'not necessarily your diagnosis' and 'stays yours' could be read as guarantees. ADA applies to US employers with 15+ employees; laws differ internationally. The 'not necessarily' hedge is doing important work and must stay in.

items.text: Most neurodivergent employees don't realize: you can often request workplace accommodations without naming your diagnosis. Describe the functional barrier. Let HR work from there.
items.rationale: Softer entry point than post 8 — 'often' is an honest hedge, and the directive structure ('Describe. Let HR work.') is low-demand. For people earlier in their thinking who need a gentler starting point.
items.sensitivity_flag: Same jurisdiction caveat as post 8 — US-ADA framing. 'Often' is correctly hedged. Pairing posts 8 and 9 on the same day risks redundancy; pick one.

items.text: Low-demand parenting doesn't fail because the approach is wrong. It fails when the adult holding the space has no support for their own nervous system. You can't co-regulate from empty.
items.rationale: Externalises a guilt trap embedded in LDP discourse without dismissing the approach itself. 'Co-regulate from empty' is pithy and already community-native. Speaks directly to autistic parents raising PDA kids who are themselves in burnout.

items.text: Does renaming PDA to 'Persistent Drive for Autonomy' actually change how schools and clinicians treat PDA kids — or just how we feel about the name?
items.rationale: Frames a genuinely live community debate as an honest question, not a dunk on either side. Short and clean. Invites substantive replies rather than pile-ons because the stakes are named ('how schools and clinicians treat') without a thumb on the scale.
items.sensitivity_flag: Neutral framing is intentional but the question may still draw strong responses from 'pathological' advocates and from those harmed by that framing. 'PDA kids' uses community-native language; monitor replies for individuals who prefer person-first.

items.text: Getting a late autism diagnosis doesn't clear decades of masking debt. Years of overriding your nervous system create something like compound interest. The diagnosis is real. The backlog is too.
items.rationale: Names the specific grief of late-diagnosed people who expected relief and got more to reckon with instead. 'Masking debt' is circulating community language — not clinical, not invented. The closing rhythm ('The diagnosis is real. The backlog is too.') earns its emotional landing.
